newsitem.title: USA: U.S. 30-year bond auction seen going just "okay".
newsitem.headline: U.S. 30-year bond auction seen going just "okay".

text.p: After two disappointing auctions earlier this week, U.S. Treasury market players have low expectations for Thursday's 30-year bond sale.

Yet some dealers said despite being launched on the "13th" of the month, the 30-year could get "lucky" and garner more demand than at the three-year and 10-year note auctions -- avoiding a clean sweep of lousy auctions.
In the third and final leg of its quarterly refunding, the Treasury is slated to sell $10 billion of 30-year bonds at 1300 EST/1800 GMT.
That follows what traders described as a poor $17.75 billion three-year note auction on Tuesday and a sloppy $12 billion 10-year note sale on Wednesday.
"Although they are expensive, they should go okay," said one bond trader at a U.S.-based primary dealership. "I see reasonable demand. The when-issued 30-year looks better on spread than old bonds."

In when-issued trading at 1130 EST/1630 GMT, the 30-year bond was paying 6.6275 percent. Traders said they expected the issue to sell around current levels, though some said the market may try to push the yield to 6.64 to 6.65 percent.
A rate lower than 6.63 percent is unlikely, players said, although both the three- and 10-year note sales came at lower yields than predicted.
Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities International Inc, suggested that most demand will emanate from U.S. accounts -- dealers plus some retail buyers.
"The Japanese have no interest," he said. "Last quarter they (bought) it and got hurt...the Street took losses."
He noted that at the last bond auction in November, the bond was sold at a yield of 6.24 percent.

Meanwhile, 30-year activity was been light on Thursday morning. As of 1130 EST, volume in the when-issued bond was $170 million, while the outstanding 30-year had volume of $515 million, according to GovPX.
Verterano said activity should pick up towards the 1300 EST bidding deadline, and said he expected dealers to sell shorter maturities in favor of the bonds to extend their duration.
Some traders said that unless the auction goes very well, they expect the market to sag later this afternoon.

Also, players cited uncertainty ahead of Friday's producer price report for January, which some fear could reflect inflation pressures in the pipeline. Although inflation is deemed under control, some said the continued tight labor markets and effects from higher energy prices could show up in consumer prices, resulting in higher bond yields.
